summary: A conceptual outline of an API for GRASP, to be used by Autonomic Service Agents when they call the GRASP module to exchange messages. Because GRASP is asynchronous, the API must be adapted to each programming environment.

plainLanguage.summary: A menu of the actions a program can ask the self-managing network's messaging system to do, which each language can build its own way.

what is the grasp protocol api
subtitle: The programming interface for autonomic service agents to exchange messages.

tldr.problem: Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) need a consistent way to call GRASP protocol functions to negotiate and exchange information with each other.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8991 defines an API outline that ASAs use to request discovery, negotiation, synchronization, and flooding operations, handling asynchronous operations suitable for different programming languages and operating systems.
tldr.outcome: The API remains informational because each language and platform requires its own specific implementation; the RFC provides a conceptual framework rather than a formal specification.

facts.label: Session handle type
facts.value: Opaque structure based on Session ID and initiator IP address

today: RFC 8991 is an Informational RFC published in May 2021 and remains the current conceptual outline for GRASP API design. Language-specific and platform-specific implementations must adapt it to their environments. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol (GRASP), defined in RFC 8990, is the messaging layer for autonomous network management. Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) are programs that run on network nodes and use GRASP to coordinate with each other to solve network problems without human intervention.

RFC 8991 defines a conceptual outline of an Application Programming Interface (API) that ASAs use to call GRASP functions. Since different programming languages and operating systems have different support for asynchronous operations, individual implementations will adapt this outline to their environment.
sections.plainLanguage: GRASP is how self-managing network programs talk to each other. This document explains what buttons they can push.

sections.title: Design Assumptions
sections.content:
The API assumes that an ASA calls a separate GRASP module that handles protocol details, security, sending and receiving messages, managing discovery caches, and running negotiation loops. The ASA itself knows nothing about the semantics of specific GRASP objectives; it only knows what actions it wants to perform.

Different ASAs may use GRASP for different purposes: some only for discovery, some only as an initiator in negotiations, some only as a responder, and some for synchronization and flooding. The API must support all these patterns, including scenarios where an ASA manages multiple simultaneous negotiations with different peers for the same objective.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can ask the GRASP system to do things, but they don't need to understand how GRASP works inside. It's like ordering from a menu without needing to know how the kitchen works.

sections.title: Asynchronous Operations
sections.content:
GRASP requires asynchronous operations because ASAs often need to run multiple overlapping tasks. An ASA might negotiate one objective with one peer while discovering and synchronizing a different objective with another peer. The API supports three common asynchronous patterns: multithreading (where the operating system creates and switches between threads), event loop polling (where the API returns immediately with a 'noReply' code), and callback functions (where the ASA provides a function to call when a response arrives).

Each GRASP session is uniquely identified by a session_handle returned on the first call for that session. This allows an ASA to run multiple simultaneous sessions in parallel without confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a program needs to do two things at once, like waiting for two different answers. The API can work the way the program prefers: letting it wait with threads, or just saying 'not done yet' repeatedly, or calling a function when the answer comes back.

sections.title: Core API Functions
sections.content:
The API provides functions in several categories. Registration functions allow an ASA to register itself and the GRASP objectives it will handle. Discovery lets an ASA find peers that handle a specific objective. Negotiation functions manage back-and-forth exchanges where both sides propose and counter-propose values. Synchronization allows one ASA to request the current value of an objective from another. Flooding sends an objective to all nodes in the Autonomic Network. Each function returns an error code, with zero meaning success.

The API handles session management automatically. When an ASA first registers, the GRASP core returns an asa_handle that the ASA must present in every subsequent call. For operations that need to track state, the core also returns a session_handle. This design prevents elementary attacks where one program might try to manipulate an objective it did not register.
sections.plainLanguage: The API provides a toolbox of actions: register (sign in), discover (find a partner), negotiate (make a deal), synchronize (get the latest info), and flood (broadcast to everyone). Each action tells you if it worked.

sections.title: Data Structures
sections.content:
The key data structure is the objective, which has a name, flags indicating whether it supports negotiation and synchronization, a loop count to limit message propagation, and a value. The value is encoded in CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation), which allows the GRASP core to be completely opaque to the value's semantics. The ASA is responsible for understanding and validating the value.

An asa_locator structure describes where an ASA can be reached: an IP address, a fully qualified domain name, or a URI, together with the transport protocol and port number. Discovery operations return a list of locators for ASAs that handle the requested objective. Error codes range from 0 (success) through 38 (invalid locator), covering scenarios like registry full, objective conflicts, socket errors, loop exhaustion, and CBOR decode failures.
sections.plainLanguage: An objective is like a form to be filled: it has a name, some boxes for yes/no answers (does it need negotiation?), and a place for the actual data. A locator is like a mailing address: where to find an ASA on the network.
